headline: Discriminated Unions in TypeScript
snippet: Earlier, we looked at how custom type guards (value is Type) let you manually inspect unknown data and teach TypeScript its shape. But what if you have a set of known object types that share a common property? Enter Discriminated Unions (sometimes called tagged unions or algebraic data types). They are one of the most powerful patterns in TypeScript because TypeScript does the type narrowing for you automatically—no custom guard function required. 1. What is a Discriminated Union? A discriminated union is a combination of three things: Types with a common property (the discriminant or "tag"), where each type has a unique literal type for that property. A union of those types. A conditional check (like a switch statement) on that discriminant property. Let’s see it in action with a classic real-world scenario: asynchronous state management. 2. Practical Example: State Management Imagine you are building a component that fetches data from an API. At any given moment, your state can be in one of three phases: Loading, Success, or Error. If you lump everything into one giant interface with optional fields (data?: User, error?: string), you open the door to impossible states (like having both data and an error, or neither). Instead, model them as a discriminated union using a status tag: interface IdleState { status: "idle"; } interface LoadingState { status: "loading"; interface SuccessState { status: "success"; data: { id: number; name: string }; // Only exists on success! interface ErrorState { status: "error"; error: Error; // Only exists on error! type FetchState = IdleState | LoadingState | SuccessState | ErrorState; 3. Automatic Narrowing in Action When you consume a discriminated union, you can use a simple switch or if statement checking the status tag. Watch how TypeScript's control flow analysis automatically figures out what properties are safe to access: function renderUI(state: FetchState) { switch (state.status) { case "idle": return " Press button to fetch. "; case "loading": Loading data... case "success": return ` Welcome, ${state.data.name} `; case "error": Error: ${state.error.message} No as SuccessState type assertions, no manual in checks, and no runtime ambiguity. The literal type of status tells TypeScript precisely which branch of reality your code is operating in. 4. Pro-Tip: Exhaustiveness Checking with never What happens if you add a new state later (like RetryingState), but forget to update your switch statement? In JavaScript, your UI might silently fail or render nothing. You can force TypeScript to catch missing cases at compile time using the never type: Summary Custom Type Guards are your best tool when dealing with untrusted, unstructured data coming from the outside world (unknown inputs). Discriminated Unions are your best tool when designing internal application logic, state machines, and data structures where you control the shapes.

headline: Two details worth checking in a paginated ASP.NET Core CRUD
snippet: This article was prepared with AI assistance and is based on a local ASP.NET Core and SQL Server demo. The examples are excerpts, not a complete application or a production-readiness claim. A customer CRUD can look complete when creating, editing, and deleting work from the UI. Two less visible details deserve a closer look: what happens when sort values are equal, and what happens when two requests try to create the same email address. 1. Give pagination a fully specified order The demo keeps query execution in an EF Core repository. The application service bounds the page size before passing the query to it: { Page = Math. Clamp(query. Page, 1, int. MaxValue / size), PageSize = size }; The upper page bound keeps the subsequent integer offset calculation from overflowing. Clamping is a contract choice: an API could reject invalid inputs instead, provided that behavior is documented for its callers. In the repository, each supported ordering includes the unique ID as a second key. For example: data = data. OrderBy(x => x. Name).ThenBy(x => x. Id); .Skip((query. Page - 1) * query. PageSize) .Take(query. PageSize) .ToListAsync(ct); Sorting only by name leaves the relative order of customers with the same name unspecified. Adding the ID gives those ties an explicit order. This does not make offset pagination a consistent snapshot. Inserts and deletes between page requests can still shift records. Count and item queries are separate database operations too, so concurrent writes can make their results disagree. The example does not solve either issue; those requirements would need a separate design decision. 2. A duplicate check does not enforce uniqueness The application checks whether an email already exists before saving. That gives the common duplicate case a useful response, but two requests can both pass the check before either commits. The database therefore also has a unique index on Email. Infrastructure translates SQL Server's uniqueness errors into an exception defined by Application: await db. SaveChangesAsync(ct); } catch (DbUpdateException ex) when (ex. InnerException is SqlException { Number: 2601 or 2627 }) throw new DuplicateEmailException(ex); Application handles that exception, and the API returns HTTP 409 for the duplicate email case. Application does not need to reference SqlException or EF Core. There is an important limit in this small implementation: the translation assumes a uniqueness failure during this save means a duplicate email. If another unique constraint is added, that assumption must be revisited to avoid reporting the wrong error. What was checked, and what remains open The recorded local SQL Server test submitted ten concurrent creates with the same email. It returned one 201 and nine 409 responses. The HTTP smoke test also covered CRUD, filters, sorting, and pagination. These are results from a previous local verification, not an independent installation or a complete correctness proof. The project separates domain entities, application services and interfaces, infrastructure implementations, and API composition. That separation makes the SQL-specific translation easy to locate. It does not remove the need to test the behavior against SQL Server. For a small business application, when would you move from offset pagination to keyset pagination? headline: New DWP bank checks aim to save £1.2bn by tackling benefit fraud and errors
snippet: The new system covers Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance. The DWP estimates that fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad cost £1.5bn in 2025-26. The eligibility verification measure is expected to generate £1.2bn in savings by 2030-31. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has issued its first Eligibility Verification Notice, requiring banks and other financial institutions to check information relating to certain benefit-receiving accounts as part of a new effort to tackle fraud and incorrect payments. The system applies to Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance (ESA). It is designed to identify cases where claimants may have savings that affect their entitlement or have spent longer abroad than benefit rules permit. However, the new powers do not give DWP officials direct access to people's bank accounts, transaction histories or spending habits. Instead, financial institutions will be asked to check relevant accounts against specified eligibility criteria and flag cases that may require further investigation. A flag does not mean that someone has committed fraud or broken benefit rules. The Government has also stressed that no decision about a person's benefit entitlement can be made solely on the information supplied through the system. Undeclared savings and overseas stays under scrutiny Undeclared savings and the time claimants spend outside the UK are among the areas targeted by the new checks. The DWP estimates that fraud and error involving undeclared savings and time spent abroad in relation to Universal Credit and Pension Credit cost taxpayers £1.5bn in 2025-26. The Eligibility Verification Measure is expected to deliver £1.2bn in savings by 2030-31. Minister for Innovation, Fraud and Debt Lilian Greenwood said: “Benefit fraudsters should be looking over their shoulder. These new powers will help us crack down on those who deliberately abuse the system, while ensuring people receive the right support at the right time. “We are not interested in where people do their weekly shop or how much they’re spending on new clothes. Banks will simply be asked to identify if somebody may no longer meet the rules for the benefits they receive, allowing us to investigate further where necessary. “With £1.2 billion in savings expected by 2030/31, this is a major step forward in tackling fraud and error, protecting public money and ensuring support goes to those who genuinely need it.” Anyone flagged through the system will not automatically have their benefits stopped. The DWP says further enquiries will be necessary before any action is taken. The measure is initially being introduced through a test-and-learn phase and will be subject to independent oversight before any wider rollout. Wider crackdown on benefit fraud The powers were introduced under the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025 and form part of the Government's wider efforts to reduce incorrect benefit payments and protect public funds. The Government is also planning to deploy an additional 2,000 anti-fraud specialists to Jobcentres and introduce tougher checks involving Universal Credit claims from people who have travelled abroad. The wider package of measures is expected to save taxpayers £14.6bn over the next five years. For claimants, the distinction between an eligibility flag and a finding of wrongdoing will be important as the new system develops. The DWP says the checks are intended to identify cases for further investigation, rather than automatically penalise people receiving benefits.

snippet: The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) will deploy personnel to cemeteries, transport terminals, churches, and other major public areas as it intensifies security measures for the observance of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day. Police Brig. Gen. Christopher Olazo, QCPD acting district director, said the deployment will be supported by force multipliers as the district prepares for the expected influx of people during Undas 2026. Aside from cemeteries, columbaria, and memorial parks, police personnel will also be stationed at LRT and MRT stations, shopping malls, markets, and other major convergence areas. Police Assistance Desks (PADs) will be established in cemeteries and columbaria to assist visitors, while regular patrols will be conducted in residential communities to deter criminal activities and safeguard properties while residents are away. As part of its preparations, the QCPD has conducted coordination meetings with concerned government agencies and stakeholders, inspected transport hubs, and held a simulation exercise involving unattended baggage suspected of containing an explosive device at a bus terminal. The exercise aimed to assess emergency response capabilities and strengthen coordination among concerned agencies in handling potential security threats. The QCPD reminded the public to observe security regulations and local government guidelines, particularly the prohibition on bringing weapons and sharp objects, alcoholic beverages, cigarettes, vape products, gambling paraphernalia, flammable materials, and loud sound systems into designated areas. Residents were also advised to remain vigilant, secure their personal belongings, exercise caution in crowded places, and plan their cemetery visits accordingly. Olazo urged the public to cooperate with security personnel and immediately report emergencies or suspicious activities to the nearest police station, E911, or the Quezon City Helpline 122.
